title: Indexing Strategies
description: Learn B-tree, hash, composite, and covering indexes and when to apply each strategy in system design interviews.

data.text: Indexes are the single most powerful tool for improving database read performance. Without indexes, every query scans the entire table. With the right index, the same query returns in milliseconds. In system design interviews, explaining which columns to index and why shows you understand how databases actually execute queries.

B-tree indexes are the default in most relational databases. They maintain a sorted tree structure, allowing the database to find matching rows without scanning the full table. B-trees support equality, range, and prefix queries efficiently. Use them on columns in WHERE clauses, JOIN conditions, and ORDER BY clauses.

data.text: Composite indexes cover multiple columns in a specific order. The index order matters: an index on (status, created_at) efficiently finds pending orders sorted by date, but cannot efficiently filter by created_at alone. Always list the most selective or most frequently filtered columns first.

A covering index includes all columns needed by a query, allowing the database to satisfy the query entirely from the index without touching the table. This avoids random I/O on large tables. Use INCLUDE or index-only scans when your query selects a small fixed set of columns from a large table.

data.caption: B-tree index lookup flow
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Query: WHERE email = ?] --> B[Root node: compare email]
    B --> C[Branch node: narrow range]
    C --> D[Leaf node: find matching row]
    D --> E[Return row pointer to table]
    E --> F[Table fetch if covering index missing]

data.text: Indexes speed up reads but slow down writes. Every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE must also update every relevant index. On write-heavy tables, too many indexes become a bottleneck. Monitor write amplification and drop unused indexes. Many production databases accumulate unused indexes over time, so review index usage statistics regularly.

data.title: Index selectivity
data.text: Avoid indexing columns with low cardinality like gender or boolean flags unless combined with other columns in a composite index. The database may choose a full scan over a poorly selective index.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: B-tree indexes support equality, range, and prefix queries on sorted columns.
Composite index column order determines which queries can use the index.
Covering indexes eliminate table lookups for small, fixed projection queries.
Every index adds write overhead; only index columns with measurable read benefit.

items.question: When should I use a hash index?
items.answer: Hash indexes only support equality lookups and cannot do range scans. They are useful for in-memory key-value stores like Redis. Use B-tree indexes for most production databases because they support a wider range of queries.

items.question: How many indexes is too many?
items.answer: Start with indexes on foreign keys and high-frequency filters. Add more only when query plans show missing index scans. A table with five to ten well-chosen indexes is common; twenty-plus is a red flag.
